Hi Samantha — thanks for sending this over and great questions. Short answer: both lanes are viable; the right choice depends on how much legal/contract customization you need up front and whether you prefer speed over negotiated economics. Below is a concise comparison and a recommended phased approach.

Marketplace (Private Offer) — pros & cons:
- Pros: fastest procurement path if your procurement team accepts Private Offers; PO-based purchase flows into your finance system quickly; metered billing allows low-friction pilots; AWS handles invoicing if they're seller of record.
- Cons: discounts are usually smaller unless we commit to a private offer with a SKU/commit; some marketplace purchases have limitations on who can be seller of record vs reseller which can affect co-sell credit timing.

Direct Contract (MSA + Purchase Order or SOW) — pros & cons:
- Pros: full control over commercial terms (SLA credits, indemnities, data handling, fixed committed discounts, reserved SKUs for capacity). Preferred if you need a tailored DPA or custom security commitments.
- Cons: longer legal timeline (often 2–6 weeks depending on redlines), procurement PO routing can be slower for initial pilots.

Healthcare-specific notes:
- DPA & data residency: we can attach the same DPA for both marketplace private offers and direct contracts. However, the marketplace path sometimes requires the vendor (Redwood) to be seller of record which changes where the invoice originates; it does not inherently change hosting or data residency. For strict on-prem or managed VPC requirements, the private deployment agreement (private + on-prem) is typically handled via a direct contract.
- Co-sell: you can preserve co-sell motions with marketplace private offers, but we need to set the correct partner mapping and PO flow so that co-sell crediting happens at the right time. That is an operational step we do with your seller/partner contact.

Recommended phased approach for Orpheus Health (short pilot + optional move to committed):
1) Pilot via AWS Marketplace Private Offer (fastest): we publish a private offer tied to a metered SKU so you can start within ~3–7 business days once procurement signs the PO. We set short-term pricing and enable telemetry for cost/usage.
2) Run pilot (60–90 days): collect usage patterns and quality signals.
3) If you need guaranteed throughput/discounts after pilot, sign a direct reserved capacity or committed spend agreement (MSA + PO) — this transition can be done while preserving historical usage for SOW.

Estimated timelines:
- Marketplace Private Offer: 3–10 business days to enable the private offer + PO processing (quicker if procurement has marketplace experience).
- Direct contract (MSA + SOW): 2–6 weeks (depends on legal review depth).

I've attached a short term sheet and a checklist of items procurement typically needs for a private offer. Happy to jump on a call with procurement to walk through the PO fields they need.

Hi Samantha / procurement team — adding operational detail from a procurement/finance perspective.

SKU & billing notes:
- For a pilot we usually publish a metered SKU (no upfront commitment). PO should reference SKU: RW-MTR-PILOT-2027 and include the AWS Account ID (if you want AWS-invoice flow) OR Redwood vendor remit (if you prefer vendor invoice).
- If you want prepaid committed discounts later, we publish a reserved SKU (RW-RES-XXXX) and map that to your account during transition.

Private Offer information we need for a smooth PO flow:
- Exact legal entity name on the PO
- Billing address & remit-to (for vendor invoice) OR AWS marketplace account ID (for AWS invoice)
- PO number format and approver contact
- Any tax-exempt documentation (if applicable)

Marketplace benefits for pilot:
- You can start usage sooner (no MSA signature required for metered pilots in most cases).
- Metered billing gives granular, usage-based invoices which is helpful for initial evaluation and cost attribution.

Potential downside to watch:
- If your procurement insists on custom MSA terms (DPA changes, indemnity, specific audit rights) we should surface those early — they may push us to the direct contract lane.

Fallback recommended by Redwood for healthcare customers wanting speed + future flexibility:
- Start on a Private Offer metered SKU (pilot) while we run a concurrent MSA review in parallel. If the MSA needs substantive redlines we can pause conversion to reserved SKUs until legal and procurement sign off.

Happy to take procurement's PO template and draft the exact line items for you.

Thanks,

Hi Samantha / Procurement team — finance here. A few notes on invoicing and revenue recognition that should help you pick the fastest path for the pilot: 

If you select Marketplace (AWS invoice):
- AWS will be the invoice issuer (seller of record) in many private offer scenarios. That means Orpheus pays AWS and AWS pays Redwood. This is the fastest path for PO issuance in many procurement systems.
- For revenue recognition we book once AWS remits; the process is standard and won't impact billing cadence on your side.

If you select Vendor invoice (Redwood invoice via Private Offer or direct contract):
- We invoice directly to the PO and can accommodate net-30 or net-45 depending on your standard terms and credit checks.
- For booked discounts tied to committed spend, vendor invoices make it easier to apply credits and reconciliations.

Recommendation for a pilot: choose the AWS Marketplace private offer if your procurement team prioritizes quick PO processing and you can accept AWS as seller of record. If Orpheus needs specific tax or remit controls, choose vendor invoice and we will accelerate our internal approval.
